newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-U.S. SPRINTERS RETURNING TO FUNDAMENTALS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-U.S. SPRINTERS RETURNING TO FUNDAMENTALS.

text.p: Top U.S. coach John Smith offers a simple explanation for the sudden resurgence in American sprinting.

"It's timing," Smith said on Monday, the day after Maurice Greene and Marion Jones clinched a golden double for the United States in the 100 metres at the world championships here. "We have got back to basic fundamentals."
Smith said young American sprinters were learning how to run properly and then seeking to emulate nine times Olympic champion Carl Lewis now that he was easing towards retirement.
Damaged pride has also had an effect. Not since the 1984 Olympics in Los Angeles had U.S. sprinters crossed the finish line first in both the men's and women's 100 metres at a major championship.

"It hurt a lot to watch the United States win neither the 100 nor the (4x100-metre) relay at Atlanta," Greene said. "I wish I had been there to do something about it, I'm there now, and it's time to change some of those things."
Greene took the first step on Monday by defeating Canadian world record holder Donovan Bailey, the source of much humiliation for American athletics fans in recent years.

Not only had Bailey won the 100 metres at the 1995 world championships and at last year's Olympics, but he had defeated the double Olympic champion Michael Johnson in their 150 metres showdown at Toronto on June 1.
"Certain people north of the border were talking about how they were going to put us in our place again," Smith said.
"But Maurice was bold enough to say, 'If you want us, come check us.'"
Check number two will come on Sunday when the Americans, with Greene running anchor, seek to end Canada's recent domination of the 4x100-metre relay.
"It's going to be fun," said Greene, who hopes to take Bailey's 100 metres world record before the northern summer ends.

Jones, who has been playing basketball for the past four years, also hopes to claim a world record over 100 metres but the 21-year-old sees Florence Griffith Joyner's record of 10.49 seconds as a long range project.
The two victors differed on whether their golden runs would have a long-term effect on the sport in the United States.
"It is going to take more than two world champions," said Jones. "We have had great sprinters in the past. But look at the (sparsely attended) U.S. championships."
Greene, however, said the victories "will help the U.S. a great deal".
"Track and field is not as big in the United States, but we are trying to make it grow as big as possible. Try to get it known as big as football and basketball."
Such interest would be sweet music to the ears of world athletics chief Primo Nebiolo, who noted on Monday that "the U.S. have taken revenge after losing the 100 in Atlanta".
"We need the United States," said the president of the International Amateur Athletic Federation. "Without the United States, athletics is not athletics."
